dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.subtitle: What the server is doing right now.
dashboard.trafficHistoryHint: Every client's transfer together, counted on UTC days.
dashboard.tunnelUptimeUnknownHint: The collector has not reported yet.
dashboard.hostUptimeHint: How long the machine itself has been running. A reboot restarts this and the tunnel with it; restarting the tunnel restarts only the tunnel.
dashboard.downloadHint: Data the server is sending to clients.
dashboard.uploadHint: Data clients are sending to the server.
dashboard.memoryBreakdownHint: What the tunnel costs against what the panel that manages it costs. VPN core is the kernel module's own compiled size, so it stays put between polls: what the tunnel allocates per client lands in kernel memory that is billed to no module, and is left out rather than guessed at. Panel is its web workers and collector together, counted so that pages a worker shares with its parent are not counted twice. Both are floors, and neither is a slice of the memory bar above.
dashboard.swapHint: Disk the machine is using as memory, because it ran out of the real thing. Some swapping is normal and costs nothing; a swap area filling up on a small server is the last warning before the kernel starts killing processes to get memory back.
dashboard.diskSpaceHint: How full the disk the server runs from is. The bar is what an ordinary process may still write, which is what df reports and is a little less than the whole disk: a filesystem keeps a reserve only root can use. A server that fills this up stops recording traffic and stops accepting configuration changes.
dashboard.diskHint: Share of the last few seconds the busiest disk spent working, with what it read and wrote over the same stretch. Partitions and stacked devices are counted through to the hardware underneath, so a single write is counted once. A disk near 100% is what makes a server feel stuck while its processor still looks idle.
dashboard.loadAverageHint: Average number of processes waiting to run, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
dashboard.topClientsHint: By traffic in the last 24 hours.
dashboard.noTrafficHint: Nothing has gone through the tunnel since the panel started watching.
dashboard.interfaceDownHint: Nobody can connect while the interface is down. Start it from the Server page, or on the server run: systemctl start awg-quick@{{iface}}
dashboard.noClientsHint: Add your first client to get a config file and a QR code.
dashboard.liveStale: Live data is out of date
dashboard.liveStaleHint: The collector last reported {{ago}}. Check the awg-panel-collector service.
dashboard.totalTrafficHint: Everything every client has moved, all time.
dashboard.activityHint: Traffic through the tunnel over the last 24 hours.
dashboard.collectorOfflineHint: Live rates and traffic history stop updating. On the server run: systemctl start awg-panel-collector
dashboard.cpuHint: Share of processor time in use, across all cores.
dashboard.interfaceDownMenu: From a shell you can also run awg-menu and restart the tunnel under Diagnostics.
dashboard.memoryHint: Memory in use, not counting cache and buffers.
dashboard.throughputHint: Traffic through the tunnel while this page is open.
dashboard.throughputWaitingHint: The chart starts once the panel has taken a few readings a second or two apart.

clients.title: Clients
clients.subtitle: Every device that can connect to this server.
clients.name: Name
clients.ipv6LeakHelp: This client's config routes only IPv4, so anything it reaches over IPv6 travels outside the tunnel with its own address. The server has already rewritten the config — re-import it on the device to fix this.
clients.emptyHint: Adding a client generates its keys, writes its config file and gives you a QR code to scan.
clients.emptySearchHint: Try a different name, address or note.
clients.emptyFilterHint: Nothing on this server matches the filter right now. Pick another one, or clear it to see every client.
clients.removeConfirmBody: The keys are deleted and the tunnel address is freed for the next client. The device cannot reconnect unless you add it again. This cannot be undone.
clients.bulkRemoveIntro: Pick which clients to clear out. Nothing is removed until you confirm.
clients.bulkRemoveExpiredHint: Their expiry date has passed. A lapsed client you switched back on is left where it is.
clients.bulkRemoveDisabledHint: Removes the ones that reached their data limit, plus the ones switched off by hand.
clients.bulkRemoveNothing: Pick at least one of the two.
clients.bulkRemoveConfirmExpiredBody: Every client whose expiry date has passed is deleted: the keys go with them and their tunnel addresses are freed for the next client. Clients still inside their date are left alone, and so is any lapsed client you have switched back on. This cannot be undone.
clients.bulkRemoveConfirmDisabledBody: Every client that has stopped working is deleted — switched off by you, switched off for its data limit, or already past that limit and about to be. Their keys go with them and their tunnel addresses are freed for the next client. Clients that are still working are left alone. This cannot be undone.
clients.bulkRemoveConfirmBothBody: Every expired client and every client that has stopped working is deleted: the keys go with them and their tunnel addresses are freed for the next client. Clients still working and inside their date are left alone, and so is any lapsed client you have switched back on. This cannot be undone.
clients.bulkRemovedNone: There was nothing left to remove
clients.expiredKeptOn: Expired on {{date}}. You switched this client back on, so it keeps working until you change the date.
clients.scanHint: Scan this with the AmneziaWG app to import the client. The code contains the private key, so treat it like a password.
clients.keysRotatedBody: The old config no longer works. Import the new one on the device.
clients.keysFailed: Could not generate new keys for {{name}}
clients.noFreeIpsHint: Every address in {{subnet}} is taken. Remove a client, or move the server to a larger subnet.
clients.longPage: Showing all {{count}} clients on one page
clients.longPageHint: Every row on screen is redrawn twice a second as the live figures arrive, so a page this long can be slow to scroll and slow to answer a click. Show fewer at a time if it is.
clients.addSubtitle: The keys are generated on the server. Nothing you type here is secret.
clients.editSubtitle: Renaming keeps the keys and the tunnel address, so the device keeps working.
clients.nameHint: Letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, up to 32 characters. It is the file name too.
clients.nameHintSuggested: Suggested at random, and yours to change. Letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, up to 32 characters — it is the file name too. Empty the box and the server names the client.
clients.nameCollision: That name was already taken. Here is another — save it, or type your own.
clients.nameTaken: There is already a client with that name.
clients.allowedIpsHint: Which traffic the device sends through the tunnel. 0.0.0.0/0 sends everything; a single subnet sends only that.
clients.dnsHint: Leave empty to use the server default. Devices use these while the tunnel is up.
clients.quotaHint: Disable the client automatically once it has moved this much data. Leave empty for no limit.
clients.speedHint: How fast this client may go. Leave a box empty for no limit.
clients.speedHintDefaultDown: How fast this client may go. Prefilled with this server's default of {{mbps}} Mbit/s; clear it for no limit.
clients.speedHintDefaultBoth: How fast this client may go in each direction. Prefilled with this server's defaults, {{down}} Mbit/s down and {{up}} Mbit/s up; clear a box for no limit.
clients.expiryHint: Switch the client off automatically at this date and time. Leave it empty and it never expires.
clients.emailHint: Only a label, so you can tell whose device this is. Nothing is sent to it.
clients.noteHint: Anything you want to remember about this device.
clients.uploadedHint: Data this client sent to the server.
clients.downloadedHint: Data this client received from the server.
clients.publicKeyHint: The server identifies the device by this. It is safe to share.
clients.disabledQuota: Switched off after reaching its data limit
clients.disabledExpired: Switched off after its expiry date
clients.createdToastBody: Scan the QR code on the device, or download the config.
clients.disableConfirmBody: The device disconnects immediately and cannot reconnect. Its keys and address are kept, so switching it back on takes one click.
clients.enableConfirmBody: The device can connect again with the config it already has.
clients.enableExpiredConfirmBody: This client's expiry date has passed. Switching it on keeps it working past that date until you change the date, and a bulk removal of the expired clients will not take it.
clients.resetKeysConfirmBody: The old config stops working the moment you confirm. The device has to import the new one before it can connect again.
clients.resetUsageConfirmBody: The all-time upload and download totals go back to zero, which also clears any data limit that has been reached. This client's whole traffic history goes with them — every stored day and month — and cannot be brought back. The server's own totals are not affected.
clients.usageResetFailed: Could not reset the traffic for {{name}}
clients.qrUnavailable: The QR code could not be generated
clients.qrUnavailableHint: Download the config file instead and import it in the app.
clients.exportAllHint: Downloads one archive with every client config in it. It contains private keys.
clients.historyFor: How much {{name}} has moved, day by day and month by month.
clients.downloadFailed: Could not download the config for {{name}}

server.title: Server
server.subtitle: Where the tunnel listens, and the commands that run around it.
server.networkHint: Where the server listens, and what address clients are given.
server.protectionHint: How the server behaves under a handshake flood. Server-side only - nothing here is copied to a client or changes what the traffic looks like.
server.junkHint: Meaningless packets sent before the real handshake, so the first thing a filter sees is not a WireGuard handshake.
server.sizesHint: Padding added to the four handshake message types, so their sizes stop being a fingerprint.
server.headersHint: The four message type markers. Plain WireGuard uses 1, 2, 3 and 4, which is the most obvious signature there is; large random values remove it.
server.imitationHint: Packets sent ahead of the handshake that copy the shape of ordinary traffic, so the connection opens like DNS, NTP, STUN or QUIC.
server.advancedHint: Header protection, content padding and the protocol's own timers, all added in AmneziaWG 3.0. Reconfigure draws them with everything above; every client needs a 3.0 build to read them, which is what a current one is.
server.listenPortHint: The UDP port clients connect to. Changing it means every client config has to be updated.
server.addressHint: The server's own address inside the tunnel, with the subnet mask.
server.mtuHint: Largest packet the tunnel carries. Lower it if connections stall on some networks; 1372 and 1280 are the usual answers.
server.dnsHint: Name servers clients use while the tunnel is up. Empty means the device keeps its own.
server.endpointHint: The address clients dial. Leave the host empty to detect the public IP, and the port empty to use the listening port.
server.keepaliveHint: Seconds between keepalive packets. It holds NAT and firewall entries open so the server can reach the client first.
server.allowedIpsDefaultHint: What new clients route through the VPN. 0.0.0.0/0 is everything; the tunnel subnet alone is a split tunnel.
server.obfuscationHint: Everything that changes what the traffic looks like on the wire. All of it is generated for this server alone, and all of it has to match on every client.
server.reconfigureConfirmBody: Pick how much to hide and what to spend on it. Junk packets, padding sizes, header ranges, decoy packets, the header protection key, content padding and the timers are all replaced with a fresh set drawn from that band. Random packet trailers are drawn on with them: they need AmneziaWG 3.1 rather than the 3.0 the rest of the group needs. Where a header protection key is drawn too, that costs you a client on exactly 3.0 and nothing older, which the key already turned away; where the MTU leaves no room for a key, it is every client below 3.1. Clear the field before saving if that is a risk. Nothing is saved until you press Save, and once you do, every client has to import a new config.
server.reconfigureExplainBody: It draws a completely new set of values for this server: how many junk packets go out before a handshake and how big they are, how much padding each handshake packet carries, where the four header ranges sit, which protocol the decoy packets imitate, and the header protection key, content padding and timers below them. Nothing here affects throughput or latency - the values are bounded so a handshake stays cheap, and the padding on data packets always fits inside what the MTU leaves free.
server.reconfigureExplainCost: Worth doing if the current settings may have been observed, and it is the only way to stop sharing a fingerprint with another server. The cost is that every client must import a new config afterwards, so hand out the new files before you restart.
server.reconfigureFailed: Could not generate a new profile
server.reconfiguredBody: Look it over and press Save to apply it.
server.savedBody: The server config was written and a timestamped backup was kept.
server.savedRestarted: The tunnel was restarted, so the new settings are already in force.
server.applyHot: Applies right away. Nobody is disconnected.
server.applyRestart: Saving restarts the tunnel for you. Every session drops for a second or two.
server.mustReimport: Clients must import a new config
server.mustReimportBody: The settings you changed are part of every client config. Hand out the new files, or the handshake fails with no error message on either end.
server.mustMatchHint: The client has to use exactly the same value. Changing it invalidates every config already handed out.
server.serverOnlyHint: Clients neither see nor need this value.
server.importerUnsafeBody: This setting arrived in AmneziaWG 3.0 - random packet trailers in 3.1 - so both ends need a build at least that new. A peer on an older release ignores the line, and so does one imported from a .conf through the Amnezia app, whose importer drops it silently. Either way that client connects without the setting, the server refuses it, and no error appears at either end.
server.unsupportedHint: The installed kernel module or user-space tools are too old for this setting. Upgrade them, or leave it empty.
server.howItWorksBody: AmneziaWG carries the same encrypted traffic as WireGuard, then disguises how it looks on the wire. Junk packets pad out the handshake, the size and header settings change the shape of the first few packets, and imitation packets make the connection open like ordinary DNS, NTP, STUN or QUIC traffic. None of this adds encryption. Its only job is to stop a filter from recognising the protocol. Every value here has to be identical on both ends, so changing one means handing out new client configs.
server.restartConfirmBody: Every connected client drops and reconnects a few seconds later. Nothing is lost, and the firewall rules are reapplied.
server.stopConfirmBody: Every connected client drops, and none of them come back until the tunnel is started again. The panel stays reachable; the VPN does not. A reboot starts it again by itself.
server.startConfirmBody: Clients can connect again as soon as it is up. Anything switched off in the meantime - a client over its data limit or past its expiry date - stays switched off.
server.unsavedChangesBody: Leave the page and they are lost.
server.rangeHint: A single number, or a range like {{low}}-{{high}}. The kernel draws a fresh value inside the range every time it uses the setting.
server.imitationHelp: Built from tags: <r N> is N random bytes, <b 0xHEX> is those exact bytes.
server.loadFailed: The server config could not be read
server.loadFailedHint: Check that {{path}} exists and that the panel is allowed to read it.

help.closing: Everything marked as matching is copied into each client config. Change one and hand out the new files: when the two ends disagree, the handshake fails with no error message on either side.
help.mustMatch: Both ends must use the same {{keys}}.
help.noMatch: None of these has to match on the client.

step.headers: The handshake itself no longer carries WireGuard's 1, 2, 3 and 4 packet type markers, which are the easiest way there is to recognise the protocol. Each type gets its own value, or a range that picks a fresh number for every packet, leaving no constant byte to match on.
step.imitation: Nothing WireGuard-shaped goes out first. The tunnel opens with complete decoy packets that copy ordinary traffic - a DNS answer, a clock sync, a STUN probe, the start of a QUIC session - so the flow begins the way any other connection on the network begins.
step.junk: Then the real handshake leaves buried in a burst of random packets. The far end cannot parse them and throws them away, so they cost only a little bandwidth, but a filter watching for one clean 148-byte initiation sees a burst of unrelated traffic instead.
step.sizes: Finally the sizes change. A WireGuard handshake is always exactly 148 bytes answered by 92, which identifies it on its own; padding moves each packet type onto a size that means nothing. The padding on data packets applies to every packet, so it costs usable MTU.

server.noParamsHint: The panel could not read the parameter catalog from the server. Check the panel service logs.
server.rangeInvalid: Enter a whole number, or a range like {{low}}-{{high}} with the smaller number first.
server.restartPending: Saved, but the tunnel was not restarted
server.restartPendingBody: The settings are on disk; the running tunnel still has the old ones. Restart it when you are ready.

profile.legend: How much to hide, and what to spend on it
profile.standardHint: The balanced draw, and the one the help text describes. A few junk packets per handshake, padding on all four message types, and a decoy session of three to five packets. Nothing here is measurable on an ordinary link.
profile.dpiHint: Spends more of everything: more junk, larger padding and a full decoy session. Worth it where the network is actively classifying traffic and a few kilobytes per handshake is the cheap part.
profile.fastHint: The smallest draw that still hides the protocol. One or two junk packets, light padding and a short decoy session - for a metered or lossy mobile link, where every extra packet is another chance to lose the handshake.
profile.randomHint: Draws from all three bands at once. The other three are published, so a server built from one of them has said which; this one leaves nothing to recognise, at the price of not saying in advance what the draw will cost.

obfuscation.title: Obfuscation
obfuscation.subtitle: What the traffic looks like on the wire, and what it costs to hide it.
obfuscation.matchTitle: Every value on this page is copied into each client config
obfuscation.matchBody: Change one and hand out the new files before the tunnel restarts. When the two ends disagree the handshake simply fails, with no error message on either side.

statistics.title: Statistics and logs
statistics.subtitle: What the tunnel has carried, what was done to it, and what its services said.

traffic.clearConfirm: Remove every traffic figure on this server?
traffic.clearConfirmBody: Every client's upload and download totals go back to zero, and so do the server's own — today, every stored day and every stored month, on this page and on the clients page alike. There is no undo and no copy is kept: a backup holds these counters as they are now, and the file behind them is cleared with the rest. The clients themselves are untouched, keep working through it, and anyone stopped by a data limit starts again with the whole of it.
traffic.cleared: Every traffic figure is back to zero
traffic.clearedBody_one: 1 client's totals went, with {{days}} day(s) of server history. Anything moving now is counted from here.
traffic.clearedBody_other: {{count}} clients' totals went, with {{days}} day(s) of server history. Anything moving now is counted from here.
traffic.clearFailed: Could not remove the traffic figures

events.title: Activity
events.subtitle: Every change made to this server, and every one the panel made on its own.
events.clearConfirmBody: Every line goes, and nothing brings them back — this is the one thing in the panel that cannot be rebuilt from somewhere else. Nothing on the server changes: no client, key or setting is touched, and the service log beside it belongs to journald. One line is left behind, saying that you cleared the log and how much was in it.
events.clearConfirmFiltered: The whole log goes, not only the lines matching the filters above, and nothing brings them back. Nothing on the server changes: no client, key or setting is touched, and the service log beside it belongs to journald. One line is left behind, saying that you cleared the log and how much was in it.
events.clearedBody_one: 1 event was removed. The line saying so is what is left.
events.clearedBody_other: {{count}} events were removed. The line saying so is what is left.
events.clearFailed: Could not clear the activity log
events.emptyHint: Adding a client, saving the server settings and signing in all appear here.
events.noMatchesHint: Widen the search, or clear the filters to see the whole log.

serviceLog.title: Service log
serviceLog.subtitle: What the processes running this panel have written to the system journal.
serviceLog.unitHint: Straight out of the system journal, for {{unit}}.
serviceLog.emptyHint: {{unit}} has written nothing the journal still holds.
serviceLog.unavailable: The journal cannot be read here
serviceLog.unavailableHint: There is no journalctl on this server, so there is no service log to show. The activity log does not depend on it.

settings.title: Settings
settings.subtitle: How the panel itself behaves.
settings.portHint: TCP port the panel listens on. Changing it restarts the panel, so the page has to reconnect.
settings.listenHint: 0.0.0.0 answers on every interface. 127.0.0.1 answers only locally, which is what you want behind a reverse proxy.
settings.basePathHint: The panel only answers under this prefix; everything else returns a plain 404. It hides the login page from scanners, but it is cover, not a password.
settings.sessionLengthHint: How long a session lasts before you have to sign in again.
settings.pollIntervalHint: How often the collector reads the interface counters. Shorter is smoother and costs a little more CPU.
settings.onlineThresholdHint: A client counts as online for this long after its last handshake.
settings.enforceIntervalHint: How often the server re-reads every client's limits and expiry, which is what picks up changes made over SSH. A limit you change here applies at once, and a client spending its way to one is stopped within seconds - unless its limit was lowered a moment ago, and then this is the longest that can take.
settings.bandwidthHint: Turn this on to give clients a speed limit. While it is off nothing is limited and the tunnel keeps the queueing the kernel gives it - the limits themselves are kept, so turning it back on puts every one of them back.
settings.shapingOnHint: Clients with no limit of their own are unaffected in what they may transfer.
settings.defaultDownHint: What a newly added client is given. 0 means no limit. Existing clients keep what they have.
settings.defaultUpHint: The same, for what a client may send.
settings.applyAllHint: Gives every client that already exists the limit above, replacing whatever each of them has now. This cannot be undone.
settings.applyAllConfirmDown: All {{clients}} client(s) on this server will be set to {{down}}. Every limit set by hand is replaced, and there is nothing that puts the old numbers back.
settings.applyAllConfirmBoth: All {{clients}} client(s) on this server will be set to {{down}} down and {{up}} up. Every limit set by hand is replaced, and there is nothing that puts the old numbers back.
settings.wanIfaceHint: Upload only — download is shaped on the tunnel itself. Empty means whichever interface holds the default route, which is right unless this server has several network cards; the manual covers those.
settings.credentialsHint: What signs you in to this panel. Fill in your current password, then change the username, the password, or both. Whatever you leave alone stays as it is.
settings.credentialsNothing: Change the username, the password, or both.
settings.usernameHint: The name you type at the login page. Leave it as it is to keep it.
settings.usernameChangedBody: You sign in as {{username}} from now on. Other sessions were signed out; this one stays open.
settings.currentPasswordHint: Proof that it is you, whichever of the two you are changing.
settings.passwordMismatch: The two passwords are not the same.
settings.passwordChangedBody: Other sessions were signed out. This one stays open.
settings.twoFactorHint: Asks for a six-digit code from your phone after the password.
settings.scanTotp: Scan this with your authenticator app, then type the code it shows to confirm.
settings.scanTotpManual: Cannot scan? Type this secret into the app instead:
settings.twoFactorEnabledBody: You will be asked for a code every time you sign in. Keep a way back in: the server-side reset is awg-panel reset-2fa
settings.twoFactorDisabledBody: Signing in now needs the password alone.
settings.disable2faConfirmBody: The password alone will be enough to sign in. If the panel is reachable from the internet, leave this on.
settings.sessionsHint: Every browser holding a valid session for this account. Signing one out ends it immediately, wherever it is.
settings.sessionThisDeviceHint: This is the session you are reading this with. Use {{signOut}} in the account menu to end it.
settings.sessionEndConfirmBody: That browser is signed out immediately and lands on the login page. Nothing on the server changes and no VPN client is disconnected. Whoever holds the password can sign in again, so change it as well if the device is out of your hands.
settings.sessionEndedBody: It is back at the login page. Signing in again needs the password.
settings.sessionEndFailed: Could not sign that device out
settings.sessionsEndOthersConfirmBody: Every browser except this one is signed out at once. Nothing on the server changes and no client is disconnected; anyone who needs to come back signs in again with the password.
settings.sessionsEndFailed: Could not sign out everywhere else
settings.tokensHint: For scripts and monitoring, which have no browser to sign in with. A token can do everything this panel can except change the credentials that authorise it - it cannot issue another token, change the password, turn two-factor off, or restore a backup over them. It can download one, though, and that archive carries the panel's database: treat a token that has fetched a backup exactly like the password.
settings.tokensEmptyHint: Nothing can reach this panel without signing in at the login page.
settings.tokensSeeApi: What a token can reach, and how to send it, is on the
settings.tokenNewHint: The secret is shown once, on the next screen. Nothing here can show it again.
settings.tokenNameHint: What the activity log will call it. The suggestion is only a suggestion — name it after the thing that will hold it, or clear the box and the server names it.
settings.tokenNameTaken: That name was already taken. Here is another — save it, or type your own.
settings.tokenExpiryHint: A token that runs out is one you do not have to remember to clean up.
settings.tokenRenewOnUse: Reset the expiry each time it is used
settings.tokenRenewOnUseHint: A token still in daily use keeps working; one whose script was retired runs out on schedule.
settings.tokenRenewNeedsExpiry: A token that never expires has nothing to renew.
settings.tokenRenewsHint: Each use puts the expiry back to {{days}} days from that moment.
settings.tokenIssuedBody: Copy it now. The panel keeps a hash and not the token itself, so this is the only time it can be shown - a token that was not copied has to be replaced rather than looked up.
settings.tokenUsingBody: Send it as an Authorization header on any API request. No cookie and no CSRF token are needed - the header is the whole of the authentication, so treat it exactly like the password.
settings.tokenEditHint: The secret is not changed by anything here, so whatever holds it goes on working.
settings.tokenSavedBody: The secret is unchanged: whatever holds it goes on working.
settings.tokenRevokeConfirmBody: Whatever is using this token stops working at once, and there is no way to bring it back - a replacement is a new token with a new secret. Nothing on the server changes and no VPN client is disconnected.
settings.tokenRevokedBody: Anything still using {{name}} is refused from its very next request.
settings.loginRateLimitHint: After this many wrong passwords, that address is blocked for 15 minutes.
settings.tlsHint: Point these at a certificate and key on the server to serve the panel over HTTPS. Leave them empty when a reverse proxy already terminates TLS.
settings.tlsOffHint: The panel is served over plain HTTP. Your password crosses the network in the clear unless something in front of it adds TLS.
settings.configEndpointHint: Client configs are written with the address the server was set up on, which is normally its IP. The panel can hand them over with the certificate's domain instead. Nothing on the server is rewritten: the swap happens on the download, the QR code and the export.
settings.configEndpointHostHint: Leave this empty to follow the certificate ({{domain}}), so a renewal for another name is picked up on its own.
settings.configEndpointHostHintNoCert: The panel has no certificate to take a name from, so type the domain clients should connect to.
settings.configEndpointHostHintAddress: The certificate is for the server's own address ({{address}}) rather than a name, and that address is what client configs already carry. Fill this in only if clients should be handed a domain instead.
settings.configEndpointNothingToUse: There is no domain to hand out
settings.configEndpointNothingToUseBody: Set a certificate above, or type the domain here. Until then configs go out with the address the server config carries.
settings.configEndpointNothingToUseAddressBody: The certificate covers the server's own address ({{address}}), which is the address client configs already carry, so there is nothing for it to swap in. Type the domain clients should connect to, or set this back to the server's own address.
settings.configEndpointCertUnread: The certificate could not be read just now, so there is no list of names to choose from. Typing one still works.
settings.backupHint: The archive holds the server config, every client config and the panel database. It contains private keys, so keep it somewhere safe.
settings.restoreWarning: Restoring replaces the current server config, every client and all panel data. Devices whose config is not in the archive stop working. Take a backup first.
settings.restoredBody_one: One client was restored. The tunnel was restarted to pick up the config.
settings.restoredBody_other: {{count}} clients were restored. The tunnel was restarted to pick up the config.
settings.upToDate: You are on the latest version
settings.updateHint: Check for a newer stable release and install it from here. A full backup is taken first, and nothing on this server is replaced until the download has been checked against its published checksum.
settings.updateCheckFailedHint: The server could not reach the release feed. This does not affect anything running.
settings.restartNoticeBody: It will answer at {{url}} in a few seconds. Your VPN keeps running the whole time.
settings.reconnectFailedHint: Open {{url}} by hand, or check the service with: awg-panel status
settings.applyNow: Applies as soon as you save.
settings.backupContents1: The server config and its obfuscation settings
settings.backupContents3: The panel database: users, settings and traffic history
settings.backupSecretBody: The archive contains the server private key and the private key of every client. Anyone who gets hold of it can impersonate your server or connect as any of your devices. Store it the way you would store a password, and do not mail it to yourself.
settings.basePathInvalid: Use letters, digits, dots, dashes and slashes only, for example /awg/ab12cd34/
settings.collectorHint: How long traffic history is kept, and how often data limits and expiry dates are enforced. The defaults suit a small server.
settings.disable2faPasswordHint: Turning two-factor off is a password-protected change, exactly like turning it on.
settings.generalHint: Where the panel answers and what it looks like. Nothing here touches the tunnel.
settings.loginRateLimitNote: Locking yourself out is recoverable: the block clears after 15 minutes, and a shell on the server always works.
settings.reconnectCheck: Still nothing? Check the service on the server:
settings.reconnectHandoff: This page cannot check another address for you, so you will be taken there in {{count}}s.
settings.restartConfirmBody: Changing the port, the listen address, the secret path or the certificate restarts the web service. This page will reconnect at {{url}}. The tunnel keeps running and no client is disconnected.
settings.restartWarning: Saving restarts the panel web service. The tunnel is not touched, so clients stay connected.
settings.restoreSelectHint: A .tar.gz written by this panel, or an older one from when awg-menu wrote them.
settings.restoreTypeHint: Restoring replaces the server config and every client. Devices whose keys are not in this archive stop working immediately.
settings.savedEndpoint: New configs hand out {{host}}. Devices already set up keep the address they have.
settings.tlsCertHint: Full chain in PEM form, readable by root and outside /root and /home, which the service cannot see. A self-signed certificate works, and browsers will warn about it.
settings.tlsChecking: Checking that the panel can read the certificate and key.
settings.tlsExpiringBody: Renewals normally replace it well before this point, so seeing this means the renewal has already missed at least one attempt. Check the timer that owns it - for certbot, systemctl list-timers '*certbot*' and certbot renew --dry-run - and remember that an http-01 renewal needs inbound port 80 to reach this server.
settings.tlsKeyHint: The matching private key in PEM form. Keep it 0600 and owned by root, and beside the certificate rather than under /root or /home.
settings.tlsMissingCert: HTTPS needs both files. Give the certificate as well, or clear the private key.
settings.tlsMissingKey: HTTPS needs both files. Give the private key as well, or clear the certificate.
settings.totpQrAlt: QR code for the authenticator app
settings.twoFactorLostBody: If you lose the phone with the authenticator app, the password alone will not get you in. The only way back is a shell on the server:
settings.updateConfirmBody: A full backup is taken first, then the release is downloaded, checked against its published checksum and installed. Your settings, clients, keys, accounts and traffic history are all kept. It takes a few minutes: the panel restarts near the end and the tunnel drops for a few seconds, so connected clients reconnect.
settings.updateBackupHint: Taken on this server before anything was replaced. Restore it from the Backup tab if you ever need to.
settings.updateReloadBody: This page is still the previous version's. Reload it to pick up the new one.

api.title: API
api.subtitle: Everything this panel does, it does through this API - so anything on the other pages can be done by a script instead.
api.quickStartHint: Three steps, and the addresses below are this panel's own. Anything the panel can do to this server, a script holding a token can do too.
api.stepTokenHint: A token is the credential for something that is not a browser. It needs no cookie, no CSRF header and no second factor, and it can be revoked on its own without changing the password. The secret is shown once.
api.stepBaseHint: Every route hangs off this address, secret path and all. Anything outside it answers a bare 404, so a scanner that has not been given this URL learns nothing.
api.stepCallHint: One header on every request, and that is the whole of the authentication.
api.oneClient: Adding a client end to end
api.oneClientHint: The operation almost every script is written for. The peer is applied to the running interface as it is created, so no existing session drops, and the configuration comes back as a file the device can import.
api.keysWarningBody: A client configuration and its QR code both carry the client's private key, and the export archive carries every one of them. They are the only responses in this API that contain a secret at all - nothing else, listing or status, ever returns key material.
api.conventionCaseBody: JSON is camelCase in both directions. Times are RFC 3339 in UTC, unless the field name ends in a unit - `lastHandshake` is Unix seconds, because that is what the kernel reports.
api.conventionTrafficBody: From the server's point of view, matching `awg show dump`: `rxBytes` is what the client **uploaded** and `txBytes` what it **downloaded**. Anything that shows these to a person has to label them that way round.
api.conventionErrorsBody: Always `{"detail": "...", "errors": {"field": "..."}}`. `detail` is a finished sentence; `errors` names the field that was refused. Some carry a `code` as well, for a caller that has to branch on the reason rather than the wording.
api.conventionNotConfiguredBody: Every route that reads the configuration answers `503` with `code: "not_configured"` where there is none - the panel installed before the VPN, a wrong interface name, a fresh container. It is an expected state rather than a fault, and `GET server/status` keeps answering `200` throughout, because that is what somebody calls to find out what is wrong.
api.conventionCsrf: CSRF, and why a token needs none
api.conventionCsrfBody: A mutating request made with the session cookie must carry `X-CSRFToken` matching the `awgcsrftoken` cookie. A request authenticated by a bearer token carries no cookie and needs no such token: nothing can make a browser attach an `Authorization` header it was not given.
api.cookieWayHint: Only worth doing for the handful of routes a token may not touch - the password, the second factor, the session list, the tokens themselves, restoring a backup and clearing the activity log. Everything else is one header.
api.cookieWayNote: An account with an authenticator answers the first attempt with 401 and detail totp_required; send the same request again with a totp field. Five failures lock the source address out for fifteen minutes.
api.machineReadableHint: The whole API as an OpenAPI 3.1 document - which is what this page is rendered from, so the two cannot disagree. Import it into Postman, Insomnia or Bruno, or point a client generator at it; the address of this panel is already in it, so nothing needs editing first.
api.machineReadableNote: It needs a credential like everything else, and a token may fetch it - a script being written against this panel is exactly who wants it.
api.twoWays: Two ways in, and which to use
api.twoWaysHint: The panel's own pages sign in with a cookie. Anything that is not a browser should send a token.
api.bearerBody: One header on every request, and that is the whole of the authentication. No cookie jar, no CSRF token, no second factor to script around, and it can be revoked on its own without changing the password anybody signs in with.
api.cookieBody: What `POST auth/login` hands back, and what this browser is using right now. Every mutating request made with it must also carry `X-CSRFToken` matching the `awgcsrftoken` cookie. Worth the trouble only for the routes a token may not touch.
api.tokenLimits: What a token may not do
api.tokenLimitsBody: A token can do anything this panel can, except touch the credentials behind it. Issuing or revoking a token, reading the token list, changing the username or password, turning off the second factor, ending a session, and restoring a backup (the archive carries the password hash and the token table) all answer 403. Otherwise a leaked token could mint itself a permanent replacement, and revoking it would be theatre.
api.tokenLimitsBackup: `GET backup` is the one gap. The archive holds the session table, and a session key is the browser's cookie itself, so whoever downloads one can sign in as the account - past every 403 above. It stays open because a nightly copy off the box is worth having, and that file already carries every private key on the server. Revoking the token later does not take the archive back: treat a token that has fetched one like the password.
api.checkToken: Checking a token from a script
api.checkTokenBody: The token list is closed to tokens, so a script cannot read the row belonging to the secret it holds. What it can do is ask who it is: `GET auth/session` names the calling token and says when it runs out, which is the check to make before a long job rather than after it fails.
api.whatTheLogSaysBody:
Everything a token does is recorded like anything else, with one difference worth knowing before you name one. The actor on those rows is `api:` followed by the token's name - every token on a panel authenticates as the same single account, so recording that account would make the log say `admin` for work nobody was present for.

So the name is load-bearing: "nightly backup" in the token list is "nightly backup" in the log a month later. A refused token records nothing at all, deliberately - that path can be driven as often as an outsider likes, and an audit trail a stranger can grow at will is not one.
api.noMatchesHint: Try a path, a verb, or a word from what you are trying to do - "quota", "restart", "expired".
api.recipeProvisionBody:
One request per client, and that is the honest shape: each one is a config rewrite and an `awg syncconf`, so a hundred clients is a hundred of each. It is fast enough for the numbers anybody provisions by hand and it is the only way to give each client its own options.

A name already taken answers `409` rather than overwriting anybody, which is what makes the loop safe to re-run: it skips what exists and adds what does not.
api.recipeSweep: Sweep the clients nobody is using
api.recipeSweepBody:
One request, not a loop. Every client in the sweep leaves in a single config rewrite and a single `awg syncconf`, where thirty deletions are thirty of each and thirty windows in which the configuration on disk is halfway through the job.

Size it first if the number matters: `GET clients` carries `expiredCount`, `disabledCount` and `expiredOrDisabledCount`, counted over the whole server by the same rules the sweep uses. A lapsed client an admin deliberately switched back on is left alone by both.
api.recipeBackup: Copy a backup off the box every night
api.recipeBackupBody:
The one privileged thing a token is deliberately allowed to do. Restoring an archive is closed to tokens, because it replaces the database the password hash and the tokens themselves live in - but copying one off is exactly what a nightly job is for.

**The archive contains the server's private key, every client's, and the panel's own database.** That database holds the session table, so whatever holds an archive can sign in as the account as well. Wherever it is written has to be as protected as the server is, and a token that fetches one is the password rather than a revocable stand-in for it.
api.recipeWatch: Notice a change without polling the list
api.recipeWatchBody:
`GET stats/live` reads a file the collector wrote, so polling it every couple of seconds costs nothing - and it carries `confStamp`, which changes whenever the server configuration is rewritten: a client added, removed, or switched off by the collector for its data limit.

So the expensive call is made only when something moved. `?peers=` narrows the peer table, and an empty one asks for none of it, which is what a caller reading only the totals should send: on a server with a few thousand clients the difference is most of a megabyte every two seconds.

The stamp is **opaque**. Compare it with the last one seen and do not parse it; the contract is that it differs after a change and does not otherwise.
api.recipeMonitor: Check that the tunnel is actually up
api.recipeMonitorBody:
`GET health` needs no credential and says only that the panel is answering, which is what a container healthcheck wants and not what a monitoring system does: the web service can be perfectly healthy over a tunnel that is down.

`GET server/status` is the one that knows, and it answers `200` even when everything it describes is broken - which is the point, because a route that failed when the tunnel failed would give a monitor nothing to read. Watch `ts` on the live blob as well: a blob that has stopped moving is a collector that has stopped, and every rate on it is then a stale number rather than a zero.
api.recipeLimit: Give everybody the same speed limit
api.recipeLimitBody:
Bits per second, `0` for no limit. Both fields are required rather than defaulted, because a body that lost half of itself in transit must not read as "and clear everybody's upload limit while you are here".

It overwrites and there is no undo: whatever any client had is replaced. `changed` counts the rows that actually moved, so running it twice answers `0` the second time rather than the size of the server. `applied: false` with a `reason` means the numbers were stored but the kernel could not be brought into line, and the collector applies them when it can.

about.title: About
about.subtitle: What this is, and where the documentation lives.
about.tagline: A stealth VPN server that sets itself up.
about.lead: AmneziaWG is WireGuard's own cryptography wrapped in per-connection camouflage, and it is at its fastest as a kernel module - the part that has to be compiled against the kernel you run and rebuilt every time that kernel changes. This panel does that for you, and manages everything around it: clients and their QR codes, quotas and expiry, traffic history, backups.
about.docsHint: The project's own writing, kept with the code it describes. The first three open on GitHub; the last is built from the routes this panel serves.
about.whyHint: WireGuard is the fastest thing a VPN can be, and its handshake is the easiest thing on the network to recognise. AmneziaWG keeps the first and takes away the second.
about.pillarDpiHint: Every fingerprint the filters match on - handshake size, header constants, packet cadence - is randomised for this server alone.
about.pillarKernelHint: Packets are encrypted where they already live. Nothing is copied out to a process and back, and nothing waits on a context switch.
about.pillarBatteryHint: Silent when idle, and each packet is sealed once. No keep-alive chatter, and no proxy chain unwrapping and re-wrapping on the phone.
about.pillarWireGuardHint: The Noise handshake and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are untouched - stealth on top of audited cryptography, not instead of it.
about.panelGuideHint: Installing, upgrading, HTTPS, reverse proxies, and what to do when something is wrong.
about.updatesHint: What an update replaces, what it keeps, and how to go back.
about.securityHint: What runs as root and why, where the keys live, what a backup contains.
about.apiReferenceHint: Every endpoint this panel serves, searchable, built from this installation.
about.mockModeHint: The panel is running against a simulated interface. Nothing you change here reaches a real tunnel.

support.title: Support this project
support.subtitle: The panel and the script under it are free, and they stay free. This page is here in case you would like to help anyway.
support.lead1: Nobody is paid to work on this. It gets written in evenings, and it gets tested on servers rented out of pocket in the places where a tunnel like this is worth having — which is the part that costs real money, because the only way to know an obfuscation profile still gets through a filter is to keep a machine sitting behind that filter.
support.lead2: Sending something buys you nothing that is not already yours. Every feature is in the repository, every release is free, and nothing is ever held back for whoever paid. What it buys is time: another evening on the thing you asked for, and on the unglamorous half nobody thanks anyone for — answering issues, fixing the installer after a distribution changes under it, chasing the bug that only appears on one kernel in ten.
support.lead3: If money is not something you have spare, that is genuinely fine, and this page will not ask twice. A precise bug report, a translation, or telling one other person the project exists is worth about the same.
support.walletsHint: Click any address to copy it, or open its code to scan from a phone. Nothing here is tracked and no amount is too small — several small ones have covered a month of servers between them.
support.networkWarning: Two of these are the same token on different chains. Send USDT only over the network its card names: TRC-20 to the TRON address, BEP-20 to the BNB Smart Chain one. A transfer that arrives on the wrong chain cannot be recovered by anybody, here or at the exchange it came from.
support.thanks: Thank you — for the transfer if you send one, and for reading this far if you do not.
